area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why and when a wing stalls in the approach and landing configuration, predict how weight, CG, flaps, power and load factor move the stall speed, and fly a commercial-standard power-off stall to the impending or full stall the examiner asks for, recovering with the AOA, wings level, power sequence and climbing away at VX or VY.
why: Stall and spin accidents usually start with an unplanned stall at low altitude, with no room left to finish the recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The power-off stall is the approach-to-landing version of that accident, and many have happened in turns from base to final and in attempts to stop a high sink rate with pitch alone [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]]. A commercial pilot carries paying passengers into those same patterns, so the recovery has to be automatic.

prereading.what: Stalls, impending versus full stall, stall recognition, AOA indicators, stall characteristics, the recovery template and the power-off stall. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 5-12 to 5-17

prereading.what: Turning power-off stalls, secondary, accelerated, cross-control and elevator trim stalls, the common errors list and spin awareness.
prereading.label: AFH 5-18 to 5-22

prereading.what: Stall aerodynamics: CL-MAX, root-first stall design, why the nose drops, the critical AOA, ice and AOA indicators.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-25 to 5-27

prereading.what: Load factor and stalling speed, and the loads you create in a stall recovery pull-up.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-34 to 5-36

prereading.what: Flap types and how each one changes lift, drag and pitching moment.
prereading.label: PHAK 6-8 to 6-9

prereading.what: Stall and spin awareness: what moves the stall speed, distractions, contamination, recognition, recovery and secondary stalls.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C 100 to 106

prereading.what: Low and slow final approaches and the high or rapid round out: where power-off stalls happen for real.
prereading.label: AFH 9-30 to 9-31

warmup: Think first: the sample stall speed table in the PHAK says a 2,750 lb airplane stalls at 57 knots with gear and flaps down and power off. On your turning power-off stall the stall horn comes on near 62 knots and the airplane breaks at about 61. Is the table wrong, or is something else going on? List every reason you can think of before you read on.

key_terms.def: The angle of attack at which airflow separates from the upper surface and the wing stalls. A given airplane always stalls at the same AOA, whatever its speed, weight or load factor [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
The peak lift coefficient. Above it, lift drops off sharply, but the wing never stops making lift completely [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
The AOA has set off a stall warning, such as buffet, a horn or a stick shaker, but has not yet reached the critical AOA [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
The critical AOA has been exceeded. Typically an uncommanded nose-down pitch you cannot readily stop, sometimes with an uncommanded roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
A twist built into the wing so the tips fly at a slightly lower AOA than the roots, making the roots stall first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
A small strip on the leading edge that makes that part of the wing stall early, one way designers make the root stall first [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
A flap with a gap that ducts high-energy air from under the wing over the flap, delaying separation and raising CL-MAX more than a plain or split flap [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]].
VSO is the stall speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100d]]; VS1 is the same in a specified configuration [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100e]].
Knowing the gap between the AOA you are flying and the critical AOA. An AOA indicator shows it directly [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Lift divided by weight, in G. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].
Any stall that happens while the load is above 1 G, so it comes at a higher indicated airspeed than the published stall speed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
A stall that builds when full power is added for a go-around with the airplane still trimmed nose-up for the approach [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

chunks.title: The power-off stall at commercial standards

body.p: The power-off stall is practiced in normal landing approach conditions. It simulates an accidental stall on the way to the runway [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Straight ahead, it is the stall you could get by stretching a glide after an engine failure or by being low on final. In a shallow turn, it is the stall you could get by misusing the controls in the turn from base to final [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

Stalls are practiced to two levels. An impending stall is when the AOA sets off a stall warning but has not reached the critical AOA. A full stall is when the critical AOA is exceeded [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. The FAA wants the same recovery technique taught for both [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

The commercial ACS asks for something the private ACS does not. On a private checkride you acknowledge the cues of the impending stall and then recover promptly after a full stall occurs (ACS PA.VII.B.S7). On a commercial checkride you acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall, and the examiner tells you whether to recover at that first indication or after a full stall has occurred (ACS CA.VII.B.S7, S8). You must be ready to fly either one, on request.

head: Element
Private ACS
Commercial ACS
rows: Heading, straight stalls
Plus or minus 10 degrees (PA.VII.B.S6)
Plus or minus 10 degrees (CA.VII.B.S6)
Bank, turning stalls
Not more than 20 degrees, plus or minus 10 degrees, while inducing the stall (PA.VII.B.S6)
Not more than 20 degrees, plus or minus 5 degrees, until the impending or full stall (CA.VII.B.S6)
How far you take it
Acknowledge cues of the impending stall, then recover promptly after a full stall (PA.VII.B.S7)
Acknowledge cues at the first indication of a stall, then recover at the first indication or after a full stall, as the evaluator specifies (CA.VII.B.S7, S8)
Recovery and climb
Recover as the POH/AFM says (PA.VII.B.S8), then configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY (PA.VII.B.S9)
Configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY (CA.VII.B.S9)
Altitude
Complete no lower than 1,500 ft AGL (PA.VII.B.S2)

callout.text: The ACS says the examiner should not demand a set altitude loss, and should not demand that you hold altitude during the recovery from an approach to stall. Many things change the recovery altitude (Commercial ACS Appendix 3, Task VII.B note). Some altitude loss is expected [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
Application: before each stall, repeat the examiner's request back in a few words: 'Turning, full stall, recover to VY, level at 4,500.' It removes guessing in the busiest 20 seconds of the maneuver.

check.q: In a turning power-off stall, how does the commercial bank tolerance differ from the private one?
check.a: Both allow a specified bank of up to 20 degrees. Commercial is plus or minus 5 degrees until the impending or full stall; private is plus or minus 10 degrees while inducing the stall (ACS CA.VII.B.S6, PA.VII.B.S6).

chunks.title: Angle of attack: the only thing that stalls a wing

body.p: A stall happens when the angle between the chord line and the relative wind goes past the wing's critical AOA. It can happen at any airspeed, in any attitude and at any power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. A stall is caused by too much AOA, not by too little airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

As AOA rises, the lift coefficient rises to a peak called CL-MAX, then falls off sharply. The wing does not stop lifting. It just cannot make enough lift for level flight [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. The critical AOA is usually somewhere from 16 to 20 degrees, depending on the design, and each airplane has only one [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. It does not change with weight, bank angle, temperature, density altitude or CG [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]].

Why the nose drops: the center of lift normally sits behind the CG, and downwash on the tail holds the nose up. At the stall the wing's lift and the tail's down force both fade, so the airplane pitches down about its CG. That lowers the AOA, speed builds, and the wing flies again, often after losing a lot of altitude [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. That nose drop is a design feature. Do not fight it.

callout.text: With the CG behind the aft limit, the elevator may not be strong enough to lower the nose. The airplane can stay stalled until it hits the ground [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

Airspeed is only a stand-in for AOA. The published stall speed holds only for 1 G, coordinated flight, one weight and one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Change any of those and the number moves, but the critical AOA does not.

check.q: Why does a stalled training airplane usually pitch nose down on its own?
check.a: The center of lift is aft of the CG, and at the stall both the wing's lift and the tail's down force fade, so the airplane rotates nose down about its CG [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

chunks.title: What moves the stall speed: weight, CG, load factor, power, altitude

body.p: The critical AOA is fixed, but the airspeed at which you reach it is not. Here is what moves it, and which way.

head: Factor
Effect on stall speed
Why
rows: More weight
Higher [[1:246|PHAK 10-2]]
The wing needs a higher AOA to make the extra lift [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]]
Forward CG
Higher [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]
More tail down load adds to the load the wing carries, so a higher AOA is needed [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]
Aft CG
Lower, but stalls come easier
Less elevator force reaches a stall, and recovery gets harder as the CG moves aft [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]
Load factor above 1 G
Higher, with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]
60 degrees of bank in a level turn is 2 G and a 41 percent higher stall speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]
Power on
Lower than power off in the sample chart [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]
Power adds lift without more AOA, and propwash over the wing adds lift right away [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Flaps down
Flaps raise the lifting ability of the wing [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]]
High altitude or temperature
Little or no change in indicated stall speed
True airspeed is higher for the same indicated speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]
Ice, frost, snow, even bugs or mud on the leading edge
Higher
The shape of the wing changes, adding drag and cutting lift [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100k]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102]]

body.p: Read the published number with care. The 1G stall speed is usually given at maximum gross weight and maximum forward CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. That makes it the high end for straight, coordinated, 1 G flight. Lighter or further aft, the real stall comes a bit slower; any G above 1 or any uncoordinated flight changes it again.

Yaw is part of K1 too. As you add power in the recovery, engine torque effects yaw the nose left, so right rudder is usually needed [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Yaw at the stall is what turns a stall into a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

callout.text: As little as 0.8 millimeter of ice on the upper wing surface increases drag and reduces lift by 25 percent [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. Do not fly with snow, ice or frost on the airplane [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100k]].

check.q: You fly the same airplane twice: once at max gross with the CG at its forward limit, once light with the CG near its aft limit. Which flight has the higher stall speed, and which is easier to stall by accident?
check.a: Heavy and forward has the higher stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]] [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. Light and aft takes less elevator force to stall, so an inadvertent stall comes easier, and recovery is harder [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]].

chunks.title: Flaps, configuration and the stall speed table

body.p: Flaps are the most common high-lift device. Hinged to the trailing edge, they increase both lift and induced drag at any AOA, so you can cruise fast and still land slow [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]].

bullets: Plain flap: adds camber and a lot of lift, adds a lot of drag, and moves the center of pressure aft, giving a nose-down pitching moment [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]].
Split flap: a little more lift than a plain flap and more drag. Fully down, plain and split flaps add high drag with little more lift [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]].
Slotted flap: the most popular type. Air through the slot delays separation, so CL-MAX goes up much more than with a plain or split flap [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]] [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]].
Fowler flap: slides back on tracks, adding area as well as camber. Early travel adds lots of lift and little drag; the last part adds mostly drag [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]].
Any flap can pitch the nose up or down when it moves, so expect to retrim [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]].

body.p: The airspeed indicator shows the flap effect. The bottom of the white arc is the power-off stall speed in the landing configuration. The bottom of the green arc is the power-off stall speed clean, and it is the higher of the two [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100c]].

The PHAK sample table puts it all on one page. For a 2,750 lb airplane, look at how power, flaps and bank each move the number. The PHAK's own worked example: gear and flaps down, power off, 45 degrees of bank gives 78 mph, or 68 knots [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

On the checkride, the examiner picks the approach or the landing configuration (ACS CA.VII.B.S3). The AFH also says to practice power-off stalls at all flap settings, so you know how the airplane handles after a mechanical failure, icing or another abnormal situation [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

callout.text: Raising the flaps abruptly at low speed can stall the airplane [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. In the go-around after the recovery, take them up in small steps as the airplane accelerates [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: Using the PHAK table, how much does lowering the gear and flaps reduce the power-off, wings-level stall speed?
check.a: From 65 knots to 57 knots, so 65 - 57 = 8 knots [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

chunks.title: Wing design and how an airplane stalls

body.p: Different designs stall in different ways. Geometry, CG, wing design and high-lift devices all play a part, so you need to know the stall behavior of the airplane you fly and the manufacturer's recovery [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

bullets: Most trainers stall at the wing root first, and the stall spreads outward toward the tips. Washout gives the tips a slightly lower AOA so the ailerons keep some effect at the stall [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
Stall strips on the leading edge make that part of the wing stall early, another way to make the root go first [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

A rectangular wing tends to stall at the root first, gives good stall warning and good aileron effect, and is usually quite stable. That is why it is popular on low-cost, low-speed airplanes [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].
An elliptical wing is very efficient but gives little warning before a complete stall, and the ailerons may be weak [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].
A rounded, almost blunt leading edge stalls smoothly: separation starts at the trailing edge and creeps forward. A sharp leading edge stalls abruptly [[1:147|PHAK 5-50]].
Very low aspect ratio wings have high stall speeds, and with sweepback they need very precise slow-speed flying. High aspect ratio wings forgive more [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].

body.p: Root-first stalls leave the tips flying, so the ailerons keep some effect until the stalled flow spreads outward [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. But the AFH warns against using that roll control too early. If the left wing drops at the stall and you add right aileron, the left aileron goes down, raising the AOA at the left tip and stalling it more. The roll can get worse [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

callout.text: Reduce the AOA before you try to roll. Roll stability and roll control improve a lot once the wings are flying again [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Your POH stall section may describe wing drop, altitude loss in a stall, or the stall warning margin. Read it before the checkride; the examiner may ask what to expect in your airplane.

check.q: Why can right aileron make a left wing drop worse at the stall?
check.a: The down-going left aileron increases the AOA at the left tip and adds induced drag, so the tip stalls more completely and the airplane can roll further left [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

body.p: You learn the impending stall by sight, sound and feel [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Feel: control pressures get lighter, you need bigger inputs, and the airplane is slower to respond. Sound: the airflow noise changes as speed drops. Kinesthesia: the seat-of-the-pants sense of changes in speed and direction can warn a trained pilot. Vision is the weakest cue, because you can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Just before the stall, buffeting or vibration may begin [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

In a power-off stall the buffet and shaking are weaker than in a power-on stall. In a power-off 1 G stall, the main cue may be the elevator control hard against the aft stop with a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. A full stall typically shows up as an uncommanded nose-down pitch you cannot readily stop, sometimes with an uncommanded roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
Stall warning devices and their limits (R2):

bullets: The rule: an airplane must have controllable stall characteristics and a clear, distinctive stall warning with enough margin to prevent an inadvertent stall [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150(a)]].
The warning may be built-in aerodynamic buffet instead of a device. Most vintage airplanes and many light-sport and experimental airplanes have no stall warning device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Many devices alert you 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]], but that is a typical figure, not a promise for your airplane.
A stall warning system can fail, so cross-check buffet, loss of roll authority and an inability to stop a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
In icing, the stall can come with little or none of the usual cues, at a lower AOA and a higher airspeed than normal [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102b]].

AOA indicators help, but calibration, unheated probes or vanes, the type of indicator, flap setting and wing contamination can limit them. Some account for flap position and some do not [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

body.p: Stall warnings in normal operations (R3): the warning can be the first sign that energy is running out. In the AFH's high-density-altitude departure story, the airplane stops climbing as the pilot keeps raising the nose, and then the stall horn sounds [[24:101|AFH 4-15]] [[24:102|AFH 4-16]]. On a landing, the airplane is close to a stall as it reaches the landing attitude [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]. Know when a warning is expected and when it means you need to act right now.

callout.text: Over-relying on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while ignoring other cues is a listed common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Use every cue together.

check.q: What does the AFH say may be the main cue in a power-off, 1 G stall, since the buffet is weak?
check.a: The elevator control position, full aft against the stop, together with a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

chunks.title: Where power-off stalls happen for real

body.p: Loss of control is the number one root cause of fatal accidents in general and commercial aviation. More than 25 percent of GA fatal accidents happen in the maneuvering phase, and half of those involve stall or spin [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. The power-off stall is about the approach. Many stall/spin accidents have come from crossed-control turns from base to final, from fixing a high sink rate on final with pitch alone, and from poor airspeed control in the pattern [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]].

head: Situation
How it leads to a stall
Prevention
rows: Low on final
Raising the nose without power slows the airplane toward the critical AOA [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Add power as you raise the nose; do not retract flaps; go around if in doubt [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Stretching the glide
Pitch alone raises AOA and decays airspeed, ending in a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]
Fly pitch and power together; pick a reachable spot
Slow final
The wing works near the critical AOA and may stall or sink hard [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Add power early; if too slow and too low, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Overshooting base to final
Steep bank plus inside rudder plus back pressure: a skidding cross-control stall [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Go around; avoid more than 30 degrees of bank this low [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
High round out
Holding the round out increases AOA to critical and the airplane drops in [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Hold attitude, add a little power, go around if the nose must come down a lot [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]

body.p: Environment (R6):

bullets: Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly raise the AOA, and the stall often comes while you fight to hold the flightpath on a gusty approach. Carry a higher approach speed in moderate or worse turbulence or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

Microbursts: if you reduce power and lower the nose for the headwind shear, you are nose-low and power-low when the tailwind shear hits, which can cause a stall or a landing short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

High density altitude: the indicated stall speed hardly changes, so fly the same indicated approach speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. But a higher density altitude lowers the engine's power output [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]], so the power that shortens your recovery is weaker. Application: expect more altitude loss in the recovery and in the go-around.

callout.text: Prevention is energy management: a stabilized approach at the right speed, pitch and power used together, and an early go-around. The AFH's go-around order is power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. In a stall it is different: AOA comes first.

check.q: On a hot afternoon at a high field, do you fly a higher indicated approach speed to protect against a stall?
check.a: No. Altitude and temperature have little or no effect on indicated stall speed, so use the manufacturer's indicated approach speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. Expect less power for any recovery [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].

chunks.title: The recovery: AOA, then wings level, then power

body.p: The most important action in any impending or full stall is to reduce the AOA. Pilots who put power and holding altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The AFH gives a generic recovery adapted from a template written by major airplane makers. Follow your manufacturer's procedure when one is published and current [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

bullets: 1. Wing leveler or autopilot: disconnect it at once, so it cannot fight you or move the trim [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
2. Pitch nose-down until the stall warning is gone. Nose-down trim only if the elevator alone is not enough, since too much trim can make things worse [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
3. Roll the wings level to point the lift the right way, using rudder to cancel yaw so the stall does not become a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
4. Add power as needed, smoothly, with rudder and elevator to stop yaw and pitch-up. Power reduces altitude loss but does not end a stall by itself [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
5. Speed brakes or spoilers: retract, if you have them [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
6. Return to the desired flightpath with smooth, coordinated inputs, watching for a secondary stall and for terrain [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: In a single-engine trainer with no autopilot or spoilers, only four steps remain: reduce AOA until the stall warning stops, roll wings level, add power as needed while staying coordinated, then return to the desired flightpath [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. You have recovered once you are back on the desired flightpath with enough airspeed, good control response and no stall warning [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

How hard to push: just enough. Every airplane needs a different amount, and too much forward pressure can put a negative load on the wing and slow the recovery [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. Snapping the control forward can create a negative load that lifts you out of the seat [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Then the pull-up: dive only to cruise or maneuvering speed and pull up gradually once safely above stall speed, and the load should not need to go past 2 to 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

After a simulated approach stall: establish a positive rate of climb as in a go-around, then retract flaps and gear as needed [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. The ACS wants the manufacturer's configuration and acceleration to VX or VY (ACS CA.VII.B.S9). VX gives the most altitude in a given distance, used for obstacles; VY gives the most altitude in a given time [[24:78|AFH 3-17]] [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]].

callout.text: Push, roll, power: the AOA comes down first, the wings come level second, and the throttle comes third.

check.q: Which template steps does a typical single-engine trainer without an autopilot or spoilers skip?
check.a: Step 1 (disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot) and step 5 (retract speed brakes or spoilers) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: Secondary stall: you exceed the critical AOA a second time because the recovery was rushed, the nose was not lowered enough, or you tried to break the stall with power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Near the ground the urge to pull the nose up fast gets stronger [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. If it happens, do the stall recovery again [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

Accelerated stall: any stall above 1 G, so at a higher indicated airspeed. It happens most often in badly flown turns, stall and spin recoveries, pull-outs from dives, and overshooting base to final turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. These stalls tend to be more aggressive and can surprise you [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. On a power-off stall entry, pulling the nose up too fast is itself a listed common error: an inadvertent accelerated stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. A late or rapid round out can do the same thing on a real landing [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

Cross-control stall: aileron one way, rudder the other at the critical AOA. It can come with very little warning and roll toward inverted, usually the start of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. The classic setup is a tailwind on base, a late turn, an overshoot, then more bank, inside rudder and back pressure to drag the nose around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Turning power-off stalls are flown to show this. Keep the airplane coordinated and the bank constant until the stall. If it slips, the outer wing may stall first and drop abruptly. If it skids, the bank may steepen dangerously. Do not try to stall on a set heading, but expect the stall within about 90 degrees of turn, like a base to final turn [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

One more trap follows every power-off stall: the go-around. You are trimmed nose-up for the approach glide. Full power plus that trim makes the nose rise sharply and yaw left, toward another stall. Use firm forward pressure to hold a normal climb attitude and retrim [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

callout.text: Secondary and cross-control stalls are demonstration-only maneuvers; only flight instructor applicants may be asked to perform them on a practical test [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. You still need to know how to recognize and avoid them (ACS CA.VII.B.R5).

check.q: In a turning power-off stall, what does a slip at the stall tend to do, and what does a skid tend to do?
check.a: In a slip, the outer wing may stall first and drop abruptly. In a skid, the bank may increase further to a dangerous attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

body.p: A stall goes down, so look down. Before the maneuver, make sure the area is clear of traffic at and below your altitude, and that you have enough altitude to recover [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Clearing procedures should come before stalls, slow flight and all other training maneuvers. In a high-wing airplane, raise the wing toward the turn and look; in a low-wing airplane, lower it and look. Say 'clear left, right, above, below' out loud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Many programs use two 90-degree turns in opposite directions [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

Altitude: plan an entry that lets you finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL (ACS CA.VII.B.S2), or higher if the POH says so [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Use the highest terrain in the practice area, and add the altitude your airplane actually loses in a stall.

Distractions cause stalls. Pilots stall when busy with something else: finding a checklist, restarting an engine, flying a windy pattern, reading a chart, doing fuel math or reaching into the back seat [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. The FAA's most effective stall training method uses realistic distractions during slow maneuvers [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]] [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(10)]].

Disorientation: in the nose-down recovery you will feel G changes, and the seat-of-the-pants sense is a useful cue mainly for a trained pilot in visual flight [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Losing situational awareness and failing to return to the desired flightpath or follow ATC instructions is a listed common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Note your heading and altitude targets before you start, and use the horizon and the instruments together.

callout.text: ADS-B In helps you see traffic, but not every aircraft shows on it in all airspace. Do not fixate on the display [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

check.q: Your practice area has terrain up to 1,900 ft MSL. Your airplane usually loses about 300 ft in a power-off stall recovery. What is the lowest sensible entry altitude?
check.a: 1,900 + 1,500 + 300 = 3,700 ft MSL, so you finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL (ACS CA.VII.B.S2). The 300 ft figure is your own airplane's number; the sources do not give one.

chunks.title: Fly it step by step (and what the examiner checks)

body.p: A generic flow from the AFH. Your POH speeds, flap settings and recovery come first.

bullets: 1. Brief: impending or full, straight or turning, configuration, recovery speed and the altitude, heading and airspeed to return to (ACS CA.VII.B.S8, S10).
2. Clear the area at and below you; check the entry altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].
3. Gear down if retractable, carburetor heat on if applicable, throttle back, and hold altitude while slowing to normal approach speed [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].
4. Lower the nose to the normal approach attitude, extend flaps as the examiner specified, adjust pitch to hold the speed, then set idle [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] (ACS CA.VII.B.S3).
5. Stabilize the descent at approach speed, trimmed (ACS CA.VII.B.S4). Do not carry extra speed into the entry; it causes an abnormally nose-high attitude [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

6. Smoothly raise the nose to a stall-inducing attitude and hold it with elevator. Hold heading within 10 degrees, or a constant bank of 20 degrees or less within 5 degrees, coordinated [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] (ACS CA.VII.B.S5, S6).
7. Call the first cue out loud (ACS CA.VII.B.S7). Impending: recover now. Full: keep holding the attitude until the full-stall indications appear [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
8. Recover: forward pressure until the stall warning is gone, wings level with aileron and rudder, power as needed with right rudder [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].
9. Positive rate of climb, flaps up in steps and gear up as the manufacturer recommends, accelerate to VX or VY [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] (ACS CA.VII.B.S9).
10. Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the examiner gave (ACS CA.VII.B.S10).

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Clearing and altitude (S1, S2)
Area cleared; entry altitude lets you complete the Task no lower than 1,500 ft AGL
Setup (S3, S4)
Approach or landing configuration as specified, coordinated throughout, stabilized descent
Entry (S5)
Smooth transition from the approach or landing attitude to a stall-inducing attitude
Heading or bank (S6)
Heading plus or minus 10 degrees straight; bank not more than 20 degrees, plus or minus 5 degrees, turning, until the impending or full stall
Recognition (S7)
Cues acknowledged at the first indication of a stall
Recovery (S8, S9)
At the first indication or after a full stall, as specified; manufacturer's configuration; accelerate to VX or VY
Return (S10)
Back to the specified altitude, heading and airspeed

body.p: Table source: ACS CA.VII.B.S1 to S10. The ACS gives no altitude loss limit for the recovery (Commercial ACS Appendix 3).

check.q: The examiner asks for a full stall. The stall horn sounds and light buffet starts. What do you do?
check.a: Acknowledge the cue out loud (ACS CA.VII.B.S7), but keep holding the stall attitude until the full-stall indications appear, such as an uncommanded nose drop you cannot readily stop [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Recovering early is a listed common error for a full stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

body.p: The AFH lists 18 common errors in intentional stalls [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Here are the ones that cost commercial applicants most, with a fix for each.

head: Error
Fix
rows: Pulling too fast on entry, causing an accelerated stall
Raise the nose smoothly to the stall attitude and hold it [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]
Bank wanders in a turning stall
Pick the bank on the attitude indicator before the stall; hold it constant and coordinated [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Poor rudder coordination through the stall and recovery
Ball centered on entry; right rudder as power comes in [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]
Recovering before the critical AOA on a full stall
Wait for the uncommanded nose drop or roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Leveling wings or adding power before reducing AOA
Push first, then roll, then power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Releasing forward pressure before the warning stops
Hold the nose-down input until the stall warning is gone [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Too much forward pressure: low or negative G
Use just enough to unload the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]
Secondary stall during recovery
Let airspeed build before raising the nose [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Too much airspeed in the recovery
Begin the climb as soon as flying speed returns, gradually [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Forgetting to roll wings level after the AOA is reduced
Say the steps out loud: push, roll, power [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]

callout.text: Never let the airspeed or tachometer reach their high-speed red lines during a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

check.q: Name two common errors that are about the order of the recovery steps.
check.a: Trying to level the wings before reducing AOA, and trying to recover with power before reducing AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-10. Stall recovery template. (AFH 5-15)
f1.alt: A two-column table titled Stall Recovery Template. Left column lists the item, right column the action: 1 wing leveler or autopilot, disconnect; 2a pitch nose-down, apply until impending stall indications are eliminated; 2b trim nose-down pitch, as needed; 3 bank, wings level; 4 thrust or power, as needed; 5 speed brakes or spoilers, retract; 6 return to the desired flight path.

f2.caption: Figure 5-8. Critical angle of attack and stall. (AFH 5-12)
f2.alt: Three panels, A, B and C, each showing an airfoil in blue airflow with its angle of attack marked. A at 10 degrees has smooth flow over the top. B at 16 degrees shows swirls starting behind the trailing edge. C at 17 degrees shows large swirls over most of the upper surface.

f3.caption: Figure 5-11. Power-off stall and recovery. (AFH 5-17)
f3.alt: A high-wing airplane flies along a curved path: establish normal approach, raise nose and maintain heading, then when the stall occurs reduce angle of attack, roll wings level and add power as needed, then as flying speed returns stop the descent and establish a climb, maintain climb airspeed while raising gear, flaps and trim, and return to the desired flightpath.

f4.caption: Figure 11-34. Stall speed table. (PHAK 11-28)
f4.alt: Stall speed table for a 2,750 lb airplane at level, 30, 45 and 60 degrees of bank. Gear and flaps up, power on: 54, 58, 64, 76 knots; power off: 65, 70, 77, 92 knots. Gear and flaps down, power on: 47, 50, 56, 66 knots; power off: 57, 62, 68, 81 knots. Matching mph values are also shown.

f5.caption: Figure 6-17. Five common types of flaps. (PHAK 6-9)
f5.alt: Six stacked airfoil drawings: the basic section, then a plain flap hinged down, a split flap hinged from the lower surface, a slotted flap with a gap and an airflow arrow through it, a Fowler flap slid back and down, and a slotted Fowler flap with two flap segments and two airflow arrows.

f6.caption: Figure 5-63. Effect of load distribution on balance. (PHAK 5-43)
f6.alt: Two side views of a high-wing airplane. Top: forward CG ahead of the center of lift, with a stronger down load on the tail added to the gross weight. Bottom: aft CG, with a lighter down load on the tail.

f7.caption: Figure 5-14. Elevator trim stall. (AFH 5-21)
f7.alt: An airplane glides down configured for landing and trimmed nose-up, then maximum power is applied to simulate a go-around and the nose rises. Before a full stall the pilot applies forward pressure, eliminates the stall warning, sets a normal climb attitude and retrims, then returns to the desired flightpath.

scenario.title: Checkride stalls over high, bumpy ground
scenario.setup: It is your commercial checkride on a hot July afternoon. The practice area's highest terrain is 2,600 ft MSL, the density altitude at your altitude is well above standard, and there is light to moderate turbulence below the cumulus bases. Your airplane is a four-seat high-wing single with a stall horn, loaded near max gross with the CG near the forward limit. The examiner asks for a turning power-off stall to a full stall, landing configuration, recovering to VY, then level at the entry altitude.

questions.q: What is the lowest entry altitude you can accept, and what else goes into the choice?
questions.a: The Task must be completed no lower than 1,500 ft AGL, so at least 4,100 ft MSL at the bottom of the recovery (ACS CA.VII.B.S2), plus the altitude your airplane loses, or more if the POH says so [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. High density altitude lowers engine power [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]], so allow extra.

questions.q: Should you expect the stall at the speed printed in the POH?
questions.a: Not exactly. It may come a bit higher: you are banked, so the load factor is above 1 G [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], and the turbulence can suddenly raise the AOA [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. The published number assumes 1 G, coordinated flight and a given weight and CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

questions.q: The turbulence sets off the stall horn in short chirps during the setup, well before the stall. How do you treat it?
questions.a: As real information. Turbulence can raise the AOA abruptly [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. Ease the back pressure to stop the warning, keep the descent stabilized and continue only when the airplane is under control. Do not count on a written allowance: the Commercial ACS Appendix 3 note for this Task covers only altitude loss in the recovery (Commercial ACS Appendix 3, Task VII.B note).

questions.q: What do you clear, and how, before rolling into the turn?
questions.a: Traffic at and below your altitude, since the maneuver descends [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. In a high-wing airplane, raise the wing toward the turn and look, and call 'clear' out loud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

questions.q: At the full stall the right wing drops sharply and the bank goes to 40 degrees. What is your sequence?
questions.a: Reduce the AOA with forward pressure until the stall warning stops, then roll wings level with aileron while using rudder to stop the yaw, then add power as needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Using aileron before the AOA is reduced can deepen the stall on the low wing [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

questions.q: As you climb out at VY with full power, the examiner points out traffic and asks for the time. Your nose keeps creeping up. What is the hazard?
questions.a: A distraction at low speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]], with nose-up approach trim and full power pushing the nose up toward an elevator trim stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Hold the climb attitude with forward pressure, retrim, then answer: fly first.

skills.do: Clear the area before the maneuver, especially below you.
skills.practice: On every stall, make clearing turns and say 'clear left, right, above, below' out loud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Pick an entry altitude that lets you finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL.
skills.practice: Before each lesson, write down the highest terrain in the practice area and your airplane's typical stall altitude loss; work out the entry altitude on the ground [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Set the approach or landing configuration the examiner asks for and stay coordinated throughout.
skills.practice: Practice with each flap setting, not just full flaps, keeping the ball centered [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

skills.do: Establish a stabilized descent at approach speed before the entry.
skills.practice: Hold altitude while slowing to approach speed, then set the approach attitude, flaps and idle, and trim before raising the nose [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

skills.do: Raise the nose smoothly from the approach attitude to one that induces a stall.
skills.practice: Have your CFI watch the G meter or your seat pressure: no sudden pull, a steady raise and hold [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: Hold heading within 10 degrees straight ahead, or a bank of 20 degrees or less within 5 degrees in a turn, until the impending or full stall.
skills.practice: Fly turning stalls at 15 to 20 degrees with the attitude indicator as a crosscheck; your CFI calls out any bank change over 3 degrees [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Call out the first stall cue, such as buffet or the stall horn.
skills.practice: Say 'horn' or 'buffet' out loud the instant you notice it on every stall, including impending ones [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

skills.do: Recover at the first indication or after a full stall, whichever the examiner asks for.
skills.practice: Alternate impending and full stalls on each flight so you get used to hearing which one is wanted and doing exactly that [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

skills.do: Configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY.
skills.practice: Rehearse the flap and gear retraction steps and target speeds on the ground in the airplane, then fly them [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

skills.do: Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the examiner specified.
skills.practice: Write the return targets on your kneeboard before each stall and level off on them [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

quiz.q: On a commercial checkride, who decides whether you recover at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall?
options: You, the applicant
The POH
The evaluator
It is always a full stall
quiz.why: You recover at the first indication or after a full stall has occurred, as specified by the evaluator (ACS CA.VII.B.S8). The private ACS always calls for recovery after a full stall (ACS PA.VII.B.S7).

quiz.q: Why is the bottom of the white arc lower than the bottom of the green arc on the airspeed indicator?
options: The white arc is marked with power on, so the propwash adds extra lift at slow speed
Flaps raise the lifting ability of the wing, so the landing stall speed is lower
The white arc assumes a lighter weight than the green arc, so its stall speed is lower
The green arc includes a built-in safety margin above the true clean stall speed
quiz.why: The bottom of the white arc is the power-off stall speed in the landing configuration, and the bottom of the green arc is the power-off stall speed clean. Flap extension generally increases the lifting ability of the wing, reducing the stall speed [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100c]].

quiz.q: Why does a forward CG raise the stall speed?
options: It moves the center of lift forward, which makes the wing stall sooner
The tail must push down harder, adding to the wing's load
It reduces the engine power available, so the wing must work harder
It makes the ailerons less effective, so the wing needs more speed
quiz.why: With forward loading, nose-up trim gives a greater tail down load, adding to wing loading, so the wing needs a higher AOA and the stall speed rises [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]].

quiz.q: What does a plain flap do to the airfoil's pitching moment?
options: Moves the CG aft
Moves the center of pressure forward, giving a nose-up moment
Has no effect
Moves the center of pressure aft, giving a nose-down moment
quiz.why: The plain flap increases camber and moves the center of pressure aft, resulting in a nose-down pitching moment [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]].

quiz.q: Which flap type adds wing area as well as camber?
options: Plain flap
Fowler flap
Split flap
Leading edge cuff
quiz.why: The Fowler flap slides back on tracks, so it changes camber and also increases wing area [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH say to practice power-off stalls at all flap settings, not only full flaps?
options: To know how the airplane handles after a mechanical failure, icing or another abnormal situation
The checkride requires a stall at every flap setting
Because full-flap stalls are not allowed in training
Because flaps do not change the stall speed
quiz.why: Power-off stalls should be practiced at all flap settings to ensure familiarity with handling arising from mechanical failures, icing or other abnormal situations [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. On the checkride the examiner specifies the approach or landing configuration (ACS CA.VII.B.S3).

quiz.q: Which statement about icing and stalls is correct?
options: The stall may come with little or none of the usual warning cues
Ice always triggers the stall horn early, so you get extra warning
Ice lowers the stall speed, so the airplane flies slower with ice on it
Ice only matters above 18,000 ft, where the air is cold enough for it to form
quiz.why: In some icing conditions the stall may occur with little or none of the usual cues, and at a higher speed than normal [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102b]].

quiz.q: In step 2 of the stall recovery template, how long do you hold the nose-down input?
options: For exactly 2 seconds, then level the wings
Until the airspeed reaches VY, then roll the wings level
Until the impending stall indications are eliminated
Until the nose is 10 degrees below the horizon, then add power
quiz.why: Push forward to reduce the AOA until the impending stall indications are eliminated before going to the next step [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

quiz.q: What does the commercial ACS say about altitude loss in a power-off stall recovery?
options: No more than 100 ft
Altitude must be held
No more than 200 ft
No predetermined altitude loss is mandated, and holding altitude is not required
quiz.why: Evaluation criteria should not mandate a predetermined altitude loss or holding altitude during recovery (Commercial ACS Appendix 3, Task VII.B note).

quiz.q: In a turning power-off stall practice, when should the stall normally occur?
options: On a heading set by the examiner before the entry
Within about 90 degrees of heading change
After at least 180 degrees of turn from the entry
Only after the bank reaches 30 degrees or more
quiz.why: No attempt is made to stall on a set heading, but to simulate base to final, the stall should normally occur within about 90 degrees of heading change [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: On a real final you realize you are well below the glidepath in gusty air. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Raise the nose without adding power so you can stretch the glide to the runway
Retract some flaps to cut drag so that you can float much farther down the runway
Add power to hold airspeed as you raise the nose, and go around if in doubt
Lower the nose and dive for the runway, then flare to get back onto the glidepath
final_quiz.why: Apply power at once to maintain airspeed while raising the pitch attitude. Raising the nose without power makes the airplane decelerate toward the critical AOA and stall, and retracting flaps makes it sink faster. If in doubt, go around [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

final_quiz.q: At the full stall the left wing drops. You hold back pressure and add full right aileron. What is likely?
options: The left wing rises at once because the aileron adds lift to the stalled tip and ends the roll
The airplane yaws right and recovers, because right aileron levels the wings with little effort
Nothing happens; ailerons do not work at all once the wing has stalled, so the roll is unchanged
The left tip stalls more because its down aileron raises its AOA, and the roll can grow
final_quiz.why: The down-deflected left aileron increases that tip's AOA and drag, making a more complete stall and possibly more left roll. Reduce AOA first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

final_quiz.q: During an impending stall, which result would make the maneuver unsatisfactory?
options: Letting a full stall develop
Adding power after the wings are level
Losing some altitude
Using right rudder as power comes in
final_quiz.why: An impending stall is unsatisfactory if a full stall occurs, if the pitch gets excessively low, or if excessive airspeed, altitude loss or a spin is not avoided [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Some altitude loss is expected [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

final_quiz.q: Using the PHAK stall speed table, gear and flaps down, power off, at 30 degrees of bank, what is the stall speed in knots?
final_quiz.why: Gear and flaps down, power off, 30 degrees: 62 knots (71 mph) [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

final_quiz.q: You recover from a stall and the airplane is diving. What pull-up does the PHAK describe as enough?
options: A sharp pull to the horizon right away, to stop the descent and save altitude quickly
Pull up at about 4 G at once and keep it there, to save as much altitude as you can
Hold the dive until you reach VNE, then level off with a firm and steady pull to the horizon
Dive only to cruise or maneuvering speed, then pull up gradually, about 2 to 2.5 G
final_quiz.why: A recovery made by diving only to cruise or design maneuvering speed, with a gradual pull-up once safely above stall speed, can be done at 2 or 2.5 G or less [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

final_quiz.q: After a full-flap power-off stall recovery you add full power for the go-around with nose-up approach trim. The nose rises sharply and yaws left. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Apply forward elevator pressure to stop the stall warning, set a normal climb attitude, then retrim
Let the nose rise; full power will keep you flying
Pull the power back to idle and glide
Retract all the flaps at once to cut drag
final_quiz.why: Propwash and nose-up trim make the nose rise and turn left. Apply enough forward pressure to reduce the AOA and stop the stall warning, return to the normal climb attitude, and adjust trim to relieve the control pressure [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. A sudden full flap retraction can cause a loss of lift [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot loads a light single with heavy bags in the rear compartment, past the aft CG limit. What is the worst stall-related risk?
options: The elevator may lack the authority to lower the nose and break the stall
A much higher stall speed than the book value, because the tail is overloaded
The stall horn fails because the lift detector no longer lines up with the airflow
The flaps cannot extend because the extra weight at the rear blocks their travel
final_quiz.why: With the CG past the rear limit, the pilot may not be able to make enough elevator force to reduce the AOA, and the airplane can stay stalled until it hits the ground [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: In a turning power-off stall you let the airplane slip. What should you expect at the stall?
options: Both wings stall together and the nose drops straight ahead
The outer wing may stall first and drop abruptly
The bank will steadily increase toward the inside
The stall speed drops because the slip unloads the wing
final_quiz.why: If the airplane is allowed to slip, the outer wing may stall first and move downward abruptly [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: Where is clearing most important before a power-off stall, and why?
options: Above, because the nose rises and the wings block your view of the sky
At and below you, because the maneuver and its recovery descend
Only ahead, because that is the direction you will be flying throughout
Behind, because of wake turbulence from traffic that is following you
final_quiz.why: Ensure the area is clear of traffic at and below your altitude and that you have room to recover [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Losing altitude during recovery is expected [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

final_quiz.q: Turning base to final with a tailwind on base, you overshoot and tighten the turn. The stall horn chirps. What is the best immediate response?
options: Add rudder toward the turn to bring the nose around and tighten the turn
Pull back to hold altitude and keep the airplane on the final approach path
Ignore it; the horn gives 4 to 8 knots of margin, so you are still safe
Lower the nose, shallow the bank, add power as needed and go around
final_quiz.why: At the first stall indication, increase airspeed by adding power, lowering the nose and/or reducing the bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; inside rudder with back pressure sets up a skidding cross-control stall [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: To reach the stall quickly on a power-off stall entry, you pull the yoke back sharply. What does the AFH call this?
options: Good technique, since it gives a cleaner break at the stall
An elevator trim stall, a listed common error in stall entries
A secondary stall, a listed common error in the recovery
An inadvertent accelerated stall, a listed common error
final_quiz.why: Pulling too fast on the controls during a power-off or power-on stall entry is listed as a common error: an inadvertent accelerated stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Raise the nose smoothly and hold the attitude (ACS CA.VII.B.S5) [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

final_quiz.q: On final near a thunderstorm you gain airspeed and climb above the glidepath, so you pull power and lower the nose. Why is that dangerous?
options: It is not; it keeps you on the glidepath
It overspeeds the flaps
When the tailwind shear follows, you are nose-low and power-low, which can lead to a stall or landing short
It causes carburetor ice
final_quiz.why: Reacting to the headwind shear leaves the airplane nose-low and power-low when the tailwind shear hits, which makes recovery harder and can cause a stall or a short landing [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

final_quiz.q: In a retractable-gear airplane, after the stall recovery you have a positive rate of climb with full flaps and the gear down. Unless the POH says otherwise, what does the AFH recommend next?
options: Raise the gear first, then raise the flaps all at once as the airplane speeds up
Leave the gear and flaps down until you have climbed back to the entry altitude
Retract the flaps at least partly before the gear, then raise the gear
Raise flaps and gear together the instant the stall warning stops sounding
final_quiz.why: It is generally recommended that the flaps be retracted, at least partially, before the gear: full flaps usually make more drag than the gear, and the gear should stay down in case the airplane touches down [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Take the flaps up in small steps as the airplane accelerates [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

takeaways: A wing stalls at its critical AOA, at any airspeed, attitude or power setting.
Weight, forward CG, load factor and contamination raise the stall speed; flaps and power lower it.
Power-off stalls rehearse the approach: low or slow finals, stretched glides and base to final turns.
Commercial standard: bank within 5 degrees, and fly the impending or full stall the examiner asks for.
Recover in order: reduce AOA until the warning stops, roll wings level, then add power as needed.
Climb away at VX or VY with flaps up in steps, holding the nose against the trim.
Clear below, finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL, and expect distractions to set up stalls.
cfi_notes: Two FAA sources word the recovery order differently. AC 61-67C paragraph 105 (dated 2000) describes reducing the AOA, then smoothly applying maximum allowable power, then establishing straight and level flight with coordinated controls [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. The AFH stall recovery template (Figure 5-10) puts rolling the wings level before power and calls for power 'as needed' [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Both reduce the AOA first. This lesson teaches the AFH template, adapted by the POH; if a student reads the AC, show them the difference.

The 'full stall' requirement trips up private-trained pilots both ways: some always recover at the horn, others always wait for the break. Mix impending and full stalls on every flight and make the student repeat the request back.

AC 61-67C gives 4 to 8 knots as a typical stall warning margin [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]; the current rule, 14 CFR 23.2150(a), only requires a clear and distinctive warning with sufficient margin and gives no knot value [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150(a)]]. Teach the student to find the margin in their own airplane.

AC 61-67C says a 60-degree level turn raises stall speed 40 percent [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100b]]; the AFH says 41 percent [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. The square root of 2 is about 1.414, so 41 percent is the closer figure. Either answer shows the idea.

The power-off 1 G stall in many trainers is mild, with the yoke on the stop and a high sink rate as the main cue [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Students may not recognize it as a full stall. Point out the nose bobbing and descent rate so they know what 'full' looks like in your airplane.
Watch for the snatch: students who think the full stall needs a big pull end up with an accelerated stall on entry [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Have them raise the nose at the same slow rate every time.

The real-world power-off stall happens in the pattern with distractions [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. After the student is solid at altitude, add the AC 61-67C distractions, such as finding a chart item or reading the OAT, during slow descents [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(10)]].
Brief the elevator trim stall before the first full-flap power-off stall. The go-around after the recovery, with approach trim and full power, is where students lose the attitude [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
gaps: The ACS lets the examiner specify 'approach or landing configuration', but none of these sources defines the approach configuration (for example, which flap setting). Use the POH and agree on it with the examiner.
No source gives a typical altitude loss for a power-off stall in a light single. Measure your own airplane with your CFI and use it in entry altitude planning.
The stall speeds, stall warning margin, wing-drop behavior and recovery procedure for your airplane come from the POH/AFM; the PHAK table and the AFH template are generic.
The sources do not give a formula for how much stall speed changes with weight or density altitude for a light single; only the direction is stated. Use the POH stall speed chart if it has one.
No source here explains how to tell, in flight, whether an AOA indicator in your airplane accounts for flap position. That comes from the indicator's manual or the manufacturer [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

activities.title: Read the airflow at three angles of attack
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Smooth airflow attached over the upper surface
Angle of attack: chord line to relative wind
Separation beginning behind the trailing edge
Flow still attached near the leading edge
Flow separated over most of the wing: stalled

activities.title: Work the stall speed numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: PHAK stall speed table: gear and flaps down, power off, wings level is 57 knots. A level 60-degree bank is 2 G, and stall speed rises with the square root of load factor. What stall speed do you predict at 60 degrees?
items.why: 57 x square root of 2 = 57 x 1.414 = 80.6, about 81 knots [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. The table shows 81 knots [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

items.q: Same table, power off, wings level: gear and flaps up is 65 knots, gear and flaps down is 57 knots. How many knots does the landing configuration take off the stall speed?

AC 61-67C says many stall warning devices alert the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall. With the table's 57-knot stall (gear and flaps down, power off, wings level), what is the highest speed at which such a horn would typically start?
items.why: 57 + 8 = 65 knots [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]] [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. That is a typical range, not a promise for your airplane.

items.q: After a recovery you pull up at 2.5 G. The 1 G stall speed is 57 knots. Below about what airspeed will that pull stall the wing again?
items.why: 57 x square root of 2.5 = 57 x 1.581 = 90.1, about 90 knots [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. 2 to 2.5 G is the most a gradual recovery pull-up should need [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

items.q: Highest terrain in the practice area is 2,350 ft MSL. Your airplane loses about 400 ft in a power-off stall recovery. What is the lowest entry altitude that keeps you at or above 1,500 ft AGL?
items.why: 2,350 + 1,500 + 400 = 4,250 ft MSL (ACS CA.VII.B.S2). The 400 ft loss is a given for this problem, not a source number.

activities.title: True or false: wing design and the stall
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A rectangular wing tends to stall at the root first and gives adequate stall warning.
cards.why: True. It also keeps adequate aileron effectiveness and is usually quite stable [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].

cards.s: An elliptical wing gives plenty of warning before a complete stall.
cards.why: False. It gives little advance warning of a complete stall, and lateral control may be difficult [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].

cards.s: Washout gives the wingtips a higher AOA than the roots.
cards.why: False. The tips get a slightly lower AOA, so the roots stall first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

cards.s: Stall strips make the part of the wing they are on stall early.
cards.why: True. They introduce a stall prematurely, one way to make the root stall first [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

cards.s: A blunt, rounded leading edge gives a gradual stall that starts at the trailing edge.
cards.why: True. Separation starts at the trailing edge and moves forward gradually as AOA increases [[1:147|PHAK 5-50]].

cards.s: A sharp, pointed leading edge gives the gentlest stall.
cards.why: False. A pointed leading edge results in an abrupt stall [[1:147|PHAK 5-50]].

activities.title: Impending or full stall?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Impending stall: warning, critical AOA not yet reached

items.t: Controls feel light and the airplane responds slowly
The airflow noise changes as speed drops
The nose pitches down and you cannot readily stop it
An uncommanded roll comes with the nose drop

activities.title: Recover and climb away in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Push forward to reduce AOA until the stall warning stops
Roll the wings level with aileron, using rudder to stop any yaw
Add power as needed, with right rudder
Establish a positive rate of climb
Retract flaps in steps and the gear as the manufacturer recommends, accelerating to VX or VY, and trim
Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the examiner gave

activities.title: Name the stall from its cause
activities.intro: Tap a stall, then the cause that fits it.

pairs.r: Raising the nose too soon, or using power only, during a recovery
Load factor above 1 G, so the stall comes above the published speed
Inside rudder with opposite aileron in an overshooting base to final turn
Stretching a glide after an engine failure, or being low on the approach
Full power for a go-around while trimmed nose-up for the approach

activities.title: Checkride power-off stall, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are on your commercial checkride in N52GT, a four-seat high-wing single. The practice area terrain tops out at 2,100 ft MSL. You are level at 3,500 ft MSL after the steep turns.

steps.s: The examiner says: 'Turning power-off stall, landing configuration, full stall, recover to VY.' What first?
options: Start the setup right now to save time, and clear the area as you descend through the maneuver
Climb high enough that recovery ends at or above 3,600 ft MSL, then clear the area
Ask the examiner to change the request to an impending stall instead, because it is safer
Descend to get below the clouds first, then begin the setup from that lower altitude
steps.why: 2,100 + 1,500 = 3,600 ft MSL, so 3,500 ft is already too low (ACS CA.VII.B.S2). Clear at and below your altitude before starting [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

steps.s: At 4,500 ft you pull the throttle back. The examiner says 'go ahead whenever,' and you are still 15 knots above approach speed.
options: Raise the nose right now and let the extra 15 knots bleed off as the airplane slows down
Enter a steep descent to build up energy, and then start the stall setup once you level off
Add flaps right away even at that higher speed, then set idle and pitch up for the stall
Hold altitude until normal approach speed, then set approach attitude, flaps and idle
steps.why: Hold altitude while slowing to normal approach speed, then pitch to the approach attitude, add flaps and set idle [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Extra speed carried into the entry gives an abnormally nose-high attitude [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

steps.s: Established in a 20-degree left descending turn, you raise the nose. The bank creeps to 27 degrees.
options: Correct back to 20 degrees and hold it coordinated
Fine, since the bank is still under 30 degrees
Level the wings and finish the stall straight ahead
Add right rudder to hold the bank at 27 degrees
steps.why: The commercial standard is a specified bank of 20 degrees or less, plus or minus 5 (ACS CA.VII.B.S6), so 27 is out. Keep the bank constant and coordinated until the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

steps.s: The stall horn sounds and light buffet begins. The yoke is not yet on the stop.
options: Recover now; the horn is the stall
Add power to hold altitude
Call 'horn,' then keep raising and holding the attitude until the full-stall indications appear
Release back pressure to stop the horn
steps.why: Acknowledge the first cue (ACS CA.VII.B.S7), but a full stall was requested (ACS CA.VII.B.S8). Hold the attitude until the uncommanded nose drop that cannot readily be arrested [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

steps.s: The nose drops and the left wing falls to 35 degrees of bank.
options: Full right aileron and full power together
Full power first, then lower the nose
Pull back to stop the nose drop
Forward pressure until the warning stops, then wings level with aileron and rudder, then power as needed
steps.why: Reduce the AOA first, then roll wings level while using rudder, then add power as needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Aileron before AOA reduction can deepen the stall on the low wing [[24:120|AFH 5-15]], and leading with power is a common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
